hero.title: Secrets: What Must Never Go Into a Repository
hero.subtitle: A key has landed on the internet. You cannot get it back. One step still helps.

toc.bridge: The Sentence From the Git Article
toc.sort: The Step With No Way Back

lead.paragraph1: The agent has built a small tool. It uploads everything to the internet. One file is included that you never opened. The agent created it on day one. There is a key inside that file. Your tool uses the key to sign in to a service. That service costs money. Nothing crashes. No warning appears. The screen looks completely normal.
lead.paragraph2: This happens often. One company searches the internet for keys. Its program found many millions of them in 2025. That is the number from one program only. It is enough for a sense of the amount. It says nothing more. What people do afterwards matters more. Researchers have studied that.
lead.paragraph3: Keys do not belong in the code. You know that from the vibecoding article. But one question stayed open there. The question is not: how do I get this back? The question is: what does this key still open?

bridge.title: The Sentence From the Git Article
bridge.text1: One sentence appears three times in the Git article. The sentence says: you delete the file later. The saved version stays anyway. Three times you read that claim. But you never read the reason. This article starts there.
bridge.text2: Three things are missing from that sentence. Why is it like this? How far does it reach? What still helps afterwards? Each one gets a section here.
bridge.album1: You know one picture from the Git article. Git is the camera. The platform is the photo album in the cloud. An album takes pictures in. And it keeps them. That is exactly what it is built for.
bridge.album2: For one thing it has no handle. You cannot take a picture back. Other people already have it. You can delete the picture on your side. Then it is gone for you. For them nothing changes at all.
bridge.rule: One sentence holds for this article: nothing is taken out of a history. Things are only added to it.

thesis.title: What This Is About
thesis.text1: You cannot undo publishing. There is no way back. A commit has a name. The name comes from the contents. And copies leave your reach at once.
thesis.text2: One rule follows from that. Do not sort by danger. Sort by way back. Is there a way back? Then the agent may do it. Is there no way back? Then you do it yourself.

objectives.title: What You Can Do Afterwards
objectives.item1: You can decide about a value: is this a secret?
objectives.item2: You can explain: why does a commit survive the deletion?
objectives.item3: You can say: what does rewriting the history not reach?
objectives.item4: You can sort an action: is there a way back?
objectives.item5: You can use the checklist before you publish something.

secret.title: The Key Is Not in the Plan
secret.analogy1: Some things are made to be handed on. Other things are not. You cannot tell by looking. An architect files the plan with the authorities. He puts it in a display case. He sends it to three firms. That is what a plan is for. The key makes none of those journeys. It sits in a different drawer. Both belong to the same house. But only one is for passing around. The other one actually lets somebody in.
secret.analogy2: Your code is the plan. Publishing code is normal. Many people do it. Publishing the key is different. It is not a worse version of the same thing. It is a different kind of act.
secret.definitionEveryday: A secret is a value. Your program uses that value to sign in somewhere. For example at a service or a database.
secret.definitionPrecise: You do not spot a secret by its looks. You spot it by what it opens. There is a test for that. Imagine this: your project becomes public now. Public means: everyone can see it. Computers can see it too. Some of them do nothing else all day. Would any access be lost? Then this value is a secret.
secret.test: The test has one big advantage. It also works on files you do not know. You do not have to read the file. You only need to know one thing. Would access travel along with this file?
secret.ask: You do not know? Then ask the agent. Ask: what does this project use to sign in elsewhere? And which files hold those values? The answer is your list. You do not need to read code.

apiKey.label: API key
apiKey.description: Your program uses it to sign in to somebody else's service.

token.label: Access token
token.description: A pass for a short time. Short time does not mean harmless.

keyFile.label: Private key file
keyFile.description: It makes a sign-in work without any password.

database.label: Database access
database.description: Address, name, and one value. That value opens the door.

config.label: Configuration file
config.description: A file with settings. The access is written in it.

misconception1.title: It Is Only a Test Key
misconception1.text: Researchers found many keys on the internet. Almost every key belonged to one person only. So they were not sample values. They were real keys. Researchers estimate: a good 89 out of 100 finds were truly sensitive. These numbers only cover the keys that were found. The reason matters more than the number. A key does not know your project size. It only knows what it opens.

secret.lookLike: Many people think: I would see a password in the code. Sadly that is not true. These values do not look like passwords. That is why counts only cover certain keys. They do not count passwords. A password can be any string at all. So do not search with your eyes. Make sure the values never enter the repository.
secret.analogyBreak: Ask about a front-door key: how many copies are there? Somebody can tell you. A key is a thing. Things can be counted. Things can be collected. A digital key is a string. For a string that question no longer works. It multiplies when someone looks at it. Nothing goes missing on your side. So the problem is not the way back. The problem is the count. Nobody knows who has the string now.

ignore.title: The Ignore Rule and Its Limit
ignore.habit: There is one simple habit. Keys sit in a file of their own. That file is often called .env. That file is not saved with the project. The program reads it at startup. This is not a security product. It is only tidiness. But it helps a lot.

misconception.title: The File Is in the Ignore List
misconception.text: Many people then think: the file is not in the repository. The list is a file called .gitignore. But its manual says the opposite. The list only covers new files. Is Git already recording a file? Then the list changes nothing. So the rule only works forwards. The mistake is always the same one. The file was there first.

ignore.silent: Now comes the important part. The rule does not bite? Then nothing happens at all. There is no error message. There is no warning. The file stays in the status report. It looks like every other file. That is why nobody notices it. It is not invisible. It is only unremarkable.
ignore.repair: There is a repair for this. You release the file from being recorded. Then the rule works. But be honest with yourself. This only repairs the future. Whatever was uploaded stays readable.
ignore.completion: The Git article recommends the ignore list. That advice is correct. But one case does not fit a short warning. The case is: the file was already there. And that case feels safe.
ignore.twoQuestions: From now on keep two questions apart. First question: is it still being recorded? Second question: is it still in there? You can only solve the first one.

chain.title: Printed Is Printed
chain.intro: Your file is printed in the evening paper. A year later somebody goes to the paper archive. They pull that very edition off the shelf. A correction came out the next morning. The page does not show that. The correction has its own edition. It has its own date. It has its own place on the shelf. It lies beside the old text. It does not lie on top. A history is a shelf like that. Six steps show why.
chain.stepsAriaLabel: Six steps from the stored object to invalidating the key
chain.step1: An object is named after its contents
chain.link1Title: Step 1: The Name Comes From the Contents
chain.link1Hash: You may know this from the Git article. Every stored object has a name. The name is calculated from the contents. Same contents means same name. Different contents means a different name.
chain.link1: A commit is such an object. It holds the state and your message. Its name comes from these contents. Something important follows from that. You cannot change the contents and keep the name. That is why a history forgets nothing.
chain.link2: So deleting takes nothing away. You delete the file. You save the deletion. Now there is one commit more. The new commit shows the state without the file. The old commit stays exactly as it was.

misconception1.title: I Deleted the File, So It Is Gone
misconception1.text: Many people think this. Researchers observed it many times. And the keys stayed reachable anyway. The status report only shows the state right now. About the stored things it says nothing.

comparison.ariaLabel: Comparison of the current state and what stays retrievable
comparison.beforeText: Only the state right now. The file is no longer in it. So the report does not show it.
comparison.afterText: Every object that was ever stored. And that in every copy of the repository.

chain.link3: Now comes a thought from advanced users. The thought is: I will rewrite the history. That sounds good. But a rewrite changes no old commit. That is simply impossible. The reason is in step 1. A rewrite writes replacements. And it moves a pointer. The old material hangs off no branch then. But it is not gone. It stays retrievable on your machine. A program cleans up after about two weeks at the earliest. Some accounts even say months. And that is still the harmless half.

misconception2.title: I Will Just Rewrite the History
misconception2.text: This feels like the expert solution. It is also the most laborious one. But it only works on your side. It never reaches anything foreign.

chain.link4Title: Step 4: It Never Reaches the Copies
chain.fork: Two words for this. A clone is a copy on somebody else's machine. A fork is a copy in somebody else's account. A fork is made with one click. After that it is not yours.
chain.link4: Your rewrite reaches neither of them. The platform also has cached views. In a paper archive you need the edition. Here the name of the commit is enough. With it people find the old state. The platform tells you what is left. Ask the owners of the forks. But it will not say who they are.

deepDive.title: What a Rewrite Does Not Reach
deepDive.text1: The platform lists it in its guidance. Clones on other machines stay. Forks in other accounts stay. Cached views stay. And pull requests stay. A pull request is a proposal for a change. It still points at the old commit.
deepDive.text2: One point surprises most people. You have to ask every fork owner yourself. The platform gives you no addresses. Support only helps in narrow cases. It does not help when a new key is enough. So the platform itself says: replacing comes first.

chain.privateRepo: Maybe you now think: I will delete the whole repository. Or I will switch it to private. Both take it off the platform. Nothing more happens. Old clones stay. Forks stay. And whoever read the value has read it.
chain.link5Title: Step 5: A Key Is a Claim
chain.claim: Now comes the step that really helps. It changes nothing about the published value. A key opens nothing by itself. A key is a claim. The claim says: I am allowed to. The service decides every single time. It decides whether the claim still holds.
chain.lockNotKey: You cannot bring the string back. But the service can refuse it. Then it is only a string. That is the picture from the start. When a key is lost, you change the lock.
chain.where: You do not do this in your project. You do it at the service. The service issued the key. Go to your account area there. You will find two buttons. One makes the key invalid. The other issues a new one.

misconception3.title: My Project Is Tiny, Nobody Looks In
misconception3.text: Here the newspaper picture stops working. A newspaper has few readers. The internet works differently. Researchers measured the time. After about 20 seconds the search finds the value. That is the middle value. Sometimes it went much faster. Sometimes it took minutes. That only means: it can be found. It does not mean: somebody attacks. And there are programs on the internet. These programs copy public repositories. Then they search through everything. Whoever finds you was not looking for you. They look at everything lying open. And your project lies open.

chain.exampleTitle: An Example: The Timeline of One Key
chain.example: In the evening your project goes online. After seconds the search finds the value. Two hours later you notice it. You delete the file and save that. This only changes the state right now. The next day you rewrite the history. That only changes what is easy to see. All copies stay the same. Then you make the value invalid. Only that changes something for a stranger.
chain.populationIntro: How often do people take that step? Researchers counted it.

stat.label: of the secrets found were not removed in about two weeks
stat.description: And of the repositories observed, not one rewrote its history. So the cleaning up removed nothing at all. The numbers come from a study from 2019.

chain.validity: Being quick still helps. The reason is uncomfortable. If nobody replaces the value, it keeps opening. One company re-tested old keys later. Many of them still worked after years.

checkpoint1.title: Quick Self-Check
checkpoint1.item1: I can look at a strange file. I can say: is a secret inside?
checkpoint1.item2: I can say what the status report tells me. And what it does not.
checkpoint1.item3: I can explain why invalidating helps. It removes nothing either.

sort.title: The Step With No Way Back Is Yours
sort.intro: Before every handover to the agent there is a question. The question is not: how dangerous is this? The question is: is there a way back? Reversible means one thing. A second action catches the first one again. You edit a file. You edit it again. Other things are not reversible. For example: publishing, deploying, sending a message.
sort.delimitation: You may know the harness article. There is a key card in it. The card opens three doors. It does not open the fourth. That is about rights. This is about something else. It is about the same door. But about another property: does the door open again? The harness article asks what an agent may touch. This article asks what cannot be taken back.

comparison.ariaLabel: Two examples: much power and little power
comparison.beforeLabel: Example 1: much power, with a way back
comparison.beforeText: The agent overwrites your whole working folder. That needs many rights. It looks terrible. But you can restore everything.
comparison.beforeResult: The agent may do this alone
comparison.afterLabel: Example 2: little power, no way back
comparison.afterText: The agent uploads one small text file. It goes into a public repository. That needs almost no rights. Afterwards everything in this article applies.

sort.axis: Same person, same day, different answer. It is not about the size. It is about the way back.
sort.rules: Some people think: I will give the agent good rules. Then this will not happen. The harness article explains that in detail. One sentence is enough here. Even a perfect rule leaves one question open. Who performs the step with no way back? Rules do not answer that question. You answer it by keeping the step.
sort.injection: An agent reads content from your project. That content can also steer the agent. The article on prompt injections shows how.
sort.doorTitle: When a Door Stops Being a Door
sort.door: There is one moment with a door. Before that moment the door is a passage. You walk through. You come back. You walk through again. Then the door clicks. Now it is a wall with a handle. The handle belongs to the other side. Half a meter lies between the two states.
sort.doorBreak1: You can see a real door. On screen it is different. Uploading looks like saving. So you decide beforehand. Not in the moment itself.
sort.doorBreak2: A door lock is real. A label is only a claim. What that means for machines comes next.

checkpoint2.title: Quick Self-Check
checkpoint2.item1: I can sort an action: is there a way back or not?
checkpoint2.item2: I can name two reasons why a machine check is not enough.

limits.title: What the Machines Do Not Take On
limits.gate: There are checks before the upload. These checks are good. The platform has push protection. It stops an upload. And it stops it before arrival. The reason is the one from this article. Afterwards it would be in the history. For public repositories the protection is on from the start. You do not have to switch it on.

misconception.title: The Platform Scans, So I Am Safe
misconception.text: There are two limits. Both are in the documentation. First limit: the check only knows certain patterns. Second limit: a person may pass it. They only have to state a reason. This gets recorded only in some repositories. Namely where the protection is switched on for the repository. Some services also block keys themselves. But that covers certain services only. And it happens after the upload. Both things help. You cannot rely on them.

limits.bypass: The important moment is the question. The check asks you for a reason. In that moment the decision is yours. This is not an obstacle. This is exactly the right moment.

deepDive.title: How a Protocol Writes Down the Way Back
deepDive.text1: There is the Model Context Protocol. Every tool gets a label there. The label says: can this be undone? The default setting matters most. If nobody says anything, this holds: you cannot undo it.
deepDive.text2: The specification also says something important. Labels from a foreign source count as untrusted. The authors explain this in a separate text. It says: these labels are only hints. They are not a real barrier. A foreign source can also lie. So a human should stay involved. That human is allowed to say no.

close.title: Back to That One File
close.text1: The file from the start had two chances. On day one the single question: what would be given away in public? The file would have come up in the answer. On day five the second chance: does the ignore rule still do anything here?
close.text2: Has it already happened? Then exactly one step helps. It is not the step that looks like tidying up. Make the value invalid at the service. And enter a new one.
close.text3: The agent may do what you can repeat. What you cannot repeat is yours.

takeaways.containerTitle: Checklist Before Publishing for the First Time
takeaways.item1: Ask this question first. The folder goes public now. What would be given away? Your answer is the topic of this article.
takeaways.item2: Ask the agent: what does the project sign in to? Which files hold those values? The answer is your list. You do not need to read code.
takeaways.item3: An ignore rule only works forwards. It only covers new files. If it does not bite, nobody tells you. The file stays in the status report.
takeaways.item4: Did something get out? Then make it invalid first. Tidying up comes afterwards. You do this at the service. Deleting the file is only cosmetics.
takeaways.item5: The step with no way back stays yours. The agent may edit and build. You decide about publishing. Does a check ask you? Then that is your decision.

q1.question: Two values sit in your project. One is the name of a payment service. The other is a string. Your program uses it to sign in there. Which one is a secret?
q1.a: Both. Together they show exactly what your project really does.
q1.b: Only the string. It opens something. The name opens nothing.
q1.c: Only the name. It shows first where something can be taken.
q1.d: Neither. Your project is small and earns no money yet.
q1.explanation: The test does not ask about looks. The test asks: would access be lost? The name of a service opens nothing. The string opens something. That makes it a secret.

q2.question: Why can a rewrite not change the old commits?
q2.a: Because only the owners of a repository may change old commits.
q2.b: Because the name comes from the contents. New contents, new name.
q2.c: Because Git encrypts old commits. The key for that is missing.
q2.d: Because a rewrite only touches branches. Branches hold no contents.
q2.explanation: A commit is named after its contents. Change the contents and it is another object. The old commit stays next to it. So a rewrite only writes replacements.

q3.question: Two people put the same file into the ignore list. One does it before the agent creates the file. The other does it later. By then the file is already recorded. Who is protected?
q3.a: Both. The list covers the folder and not the single files.
q3.b: Only the first. The rule covers files not yet recorded.
q3.c: Only the second. An entry afterwards takes the file out.
q3.d: Neither. An ignore list is only a suggestion to the program.
q3.explanation: The rule only works forwards. It only covers new files. In the second case it does nothing. And nobody tells you. The file stays in the status report.

q4.question: A key has landed in a public repository. You notice it two hours later. What do you start with?
q4.a: I delete the file. Then the current state does not show it.
q4.b: I rewrite the history. Then the commit hangs off no branch.
q4.c: I make the key invalid. Then the value opens nothing more.
q4.d: I switch it to private. Then all the old copies are useless.
q4.explanation: Deleting, rewriting, and going private only change things on your side. For a stranger nothing changes. Only the service decides about the key. So making it invalid comes first.

q5.question: Your agent is to do two things today. It is to rename 200 files. And it is to send a prepared message. Which one do you keep yourself?
q5.a: The renaming. It touches more files. The damage would be big.
q5.b: The sending. No second step brings the message back.
q5.c: Both. Rights and way back are the same sorting in the end.
q5.d: Neither. The check in front of it decides this anyway.
q5.explanation: The renaming needs many rights. You can still undo it. The sending needs almost no rights. But it has no way back. The sorting goes by the way back.
